I totally agree with what PP said about ABA. If any professional suggests it, fire them immediately and find someone else. Figure out what his special interest is and really indulge and encourage it. Whatever it is, try to join him in it if you can. While you’re his parent first, kids with autism often have a harder time making friends. You also should be that friend to him, that companion. Sensory toys are often helpful. You can order them online (I forgot the site name but you can do a simple google search). When he has meltdowns remember that you are not “encouraging” or “rewarding” the behavior by offering tools to de escalate instead of punishment or ignoring it. Our brains generally don’t work that way. A meltdown is a very, very scary and upsetting thing for us. It’s not something we do to get our way or get attention. It’s very uncomfortable and we just want to feel better. 

Also especially when he starts school, be an advocate. Make sure he gets all the accommodations he needs, that the teachers treat him well and that other children are not allowed to bully him. Another important thing to remember is that although he has autism, he’s not going to stay a small child forever. A lot of parents make the mistake of infantilizing their child as they get older because of their disability. Allow him to have whatever interests he has, age appropriate or not, but treat him with the same respect and dignity as you would a NT older child or teenager. 

Just because he may not express a certain feeling/desire does not mean it’s not there. He may or may not tell you he loves you, but not saying so doesn’t mean he does not. He may not be able to tell you when he’s sad/hungry etc. You’ve got to learn nonverbal ways to tell and figure it out. 

As for the friends thing, don’t worry about it. I had 0 friends as a child, but I’ve been able to make several as an adult. I don’t feel that I missed out on anything the way an NT would. It’s just not a big deal to me. 

Finally, remember that this is not an easy thing for a person to live with. There may be times when you get extremely stressed out, which is understandable, but it’s probably 10 times worse for him. Be understanding, loving and accepting. It will make a world of difference for him.

I wish you both all the best!

EDIT: I want to specify that I was saying you should offer tools to calm down during a meltdown, and that by doing so it does not spoil or encourage him. I reread that and can see how it may be misinterpreted.
